prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it, which opened the field of moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: Twisted bilayer graphene is the case in this shortlist where a quantitative prediction from continuum band theory (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) was followed by an unexpected experimental discovery (correlated insulators and superconductivity, Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018) that the theory could organise. That theory-experiment link is what I weigh most. The result has been reproduced by many independent groups and in several moire materials, and it has created a tunable platform for correlated matter that did not exist before. I think it fits the tradition of rewarding new quantum behaviour in materials. It also follows the 2010 graphene prize, which showed that experiment can overturn what theorists thought possible in two dimensions. The credited names map onto a prediction, the experimental discovery and the explicit continuum-model calculation. I do not want to put the work in the 'too young' category by default: eight years of independent replication is a stronger record than some earlier prizes had.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. The pairing mechanism of the superconducting state is still debated, twist-angle disorder limits quantitative comparison with theory, and the committee could reasonably prefer to wait until the physics is better understood. There is also an attribution gap: the first experimental authors of the 2018 papers are not on the credited list, and a three-person limit cannot represent them. If those reservations carry the room, the optical lattice clock (B031) is the safer and more mature choice.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B024 first for its simple, analytically understood mechanism, but would prefer a two-person prize (MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero) because Bistritzer's share of the theory credit is a judgement call and the experimental first author is missing anyway.
responses.response: I agree that the clean mechanism is the strength of the case, and I take the point about Bistritzer seriously. I still keep him in my trio. The 2011 paper is a two-author calculation that produced the magic-angle result and the flat-band picture, and leaving out one of its two authors is hard to defend on attribution grounds. The missing experimental first author is a real problem, but it argues for caution about the whole configuration, not for cutting the theory side. I would accept a two-person fallback only if the committee decides the paper by Bistritzer and MacDonald should be credited to MacDonald alone, which I do not find convincing.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first because it is mature, theory-experiment agreement is the whole point, and independent confirmation is abundant. She places B024 sixth as possibly premature, since only about eight years have passed and the nature of the superconductivity is unsettled.
responses.response: I accept that the clock is the more mature result and that its attribution to Katori and Ye is cleaner than ours. I do not agree that an open pairing mechanism makes the discovery premature. The discovery is the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle, and it has been reproduced widely; the mechanism question concerns the explanation of one phase. We did not wait for the cuprate mechanism before recognising high-temperature superconductivity. Where I do agree is that B031 is a strong alternative, and I would not oppose it if the room moves that way. My remaining question for her is how decisive the lattice-clock step is relative to the 2005 comb prize and the ion-clock work recognised in 2012.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B031 first and B024 sixth, saying B024 is a clear case of a new regime but remains young, with the credit for the key experiment possibly including Cao and others outside the three names.
responses.response: The Cao point is fair and I raised it in my own opening. I think it is a limit of the three-laureate rule and the supplied names rather than a reason to doubt the discovery. On maturity I would ask for a concrete criterion: independent replication of the central observations and a theory that explains the main features are both satisfied here. Where we may disagree is on whether the 2018 experiment is the decisive step. I think it is, because the flat-band prediction had been available since 2011 and only the experiment showed that it mattered.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as a mature, overdue instrument advance, and puts B024 third as strongly reproduced but young and possibly premature.
responses.response: I ranked B009 fifth myself because I value what correctors enabled, and I agree the recognition is overdue. My hesitation is not about science but about category: the committee will have to decide whether this is a physics discovery or an instrument advance, and the Krivanek STEM corrector priority question is unresolved with the supplied names. I would be willing to support B009 as a second part in a two-part prize if the first part were a discovery, but I do not think it should displace a discovery as the single achievement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the superconducting pairing question as disqualifying on maturity, or only as a detail of interpretation.
Whether the three credited names, without the first experimental authors, give a defensible attribution.
Whether the pace of independent confirmation in other moire systems (for example transition-metal dichalcogenides) strengthens or dilutes the case for the original graphene discovery.
How strongly the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits should weigh against condensed-matter candidates in the same cycle, if at all.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B024. I have no known collaboration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. I chaired the 2025 committee, which is relevant to the timing of B016 but is not a personal connection that would require recusal.
